title: Christians never began in revolt
source_text: Ὁμοίως δὲ ψεῦδος τὸ Αἰγυπτίους ὄντας ἀπὸ στάσεως τὴν ἀρχὴν εἰληφέναι τοὺς Ἑβραίους, καὶ τὸ Ἰουδαίους ὄντας ἄλλους κατὰ τοὺς Ἰησοῦ χρόνους ἐστασιακέναι πρὸς τὸ κοινὸν τῶν Ἰουδαίων καὶ τῷ Ἰησοῦ κατηκολουθηκέναι. οὐδὲν γὰρ στάσεως ἔργον ἐπιδεῖξαι Χριστιανῶν ὁ Κέλσος ἢ οἱ ὁμονοοῦντες αὐτῷ δυνήσονται. καίτοι γε εἰ στάσις ἦν τῆς συστάσεως Χριστιανοῖς ἡ αἰτία, τὴν ἀρχὴν ἀπὸ Ἰουδαίων εἰληφόσιν, οἷς ἐξῆν καὶ ὅπλα ὑπὲρ τῶν οἰκείων ἀναλαβεῖν καὶ πολεμίους ἀναιρεῖν, οὔτ᾿ ἂν ὁ νομοθέτης Χριστιανῶν πάντῃ ἀναίρεσιν ἀνθρώπου ἀπηγόρευε, μή ποτε δίκαιον εἶναι διδάσκων τὸ κατ᾿ ἀνθρώπου τόλμημα τῶν ἑαυτοῦ μαθητῶν, κἂν ἀδικώτατος ἐκεῖνος ᾖ (οὐ γὰρ πρέπειν ἡγεῖτο τῇ ἐνθέῳ ἑαυτοῦ νομοθεσίᾳ τὸ συγχωρεῖν ὁποιανδήποτε ἀνθρώπου ἀναίρεσιν)· οὔτ᾿ ἂν Χριστιανοὶ οἱ ἀπὸ στάσεως ἀρξάμενοι τοὺς ἐπὶ τοσοῦτον ἡμέρους προσήκαντο νόμους, δι᾿ ὧν „ὡς πρόβατα“ μὲν ἀναιρεῖσθαι αὐτοῖς ἐγίνετο μηδέ ποτε δὲ ἀμύνασθαι οἷοί τ᾿ ἦσαν τοὺς διώκοντας. καίτοι γε βαθύτερον ἐξετάζοντα τὰ πράγματα ἔστιν εἰπεῖν περὶ μὲν τῶν ἐξεληλυθότων ἐκ γῆς Αἰγύπτου ὅτι παραδόξως ὁ πᾶς λεὼς οἱονεὶ θεοδώρητον διάλεκτον ἀθρόως ἀνείληφε τὴν καλουμένην Ἑβραίαν· ὡς καὶ τῶν παρ᾿ αὐτοῖς τις εἶπε προφητῶν ὅτι „ἐν τῷ ἐξελθεῖν αὐτοὺς ἐκ γῆς Αἰγύπτου γλῶσσαν, ἣν οὐκ ἔγνω, ἤκουσεν.“
pass_a_gloss: Likewise a lie (ψεῦδος) [is] that the Hebrews, being Egyptians, took their beginning from revolt (στάσις), and that others, being Jews, in the times of Jesus revolted against the commonwealth (τὸ κοινόν) of the Jews and followed (κατακολουθέω) Jesus. For neither Celsus nor those of like mind (ὁμονοέω) with him will be able to show (ἐπιδείκνυμι) any work of revolt of Christians. And yet if revolt were the cause (αἰτία) of the forming (σύστασις) for Christians, having taken their beginning from Jews, to whom it was permitted (ἔξεστι) both to take up arms (ὅπλα) for their own [people] (τὰ οἰκεῖα) and to kill (ἀναιρέω) enemies (πολέμιος), neither would the lawgiver (νομοθέτης) of Christians have forbidden (ἀπαγορεύω) altogether (πάντῃ) the killing (ἀναίρεσις) of a man, never teaching to be just (δίκαιος) the bold deed (τόλμημα) of his own disciples (μαθητής) against a man, even if that one be most unjust (ἀδικώτατος) (for he did not think it befitting (πρέπω) his inspired (ἔνθεος) legislation (νομοθεσία) to permit (συγχωρέω) any killing of a man whatever); nor would Christians, beginning from revolt, have accepted (προσίεμαι) laws so very gentle (ἥμερος), through which it befell them to be killed ‘as sheep’ (ὡς πρόβατα) and never to be able to defend themselves (ἀμύνομαι) against the persecutors (διώκω). And yet, examining the matters more deeply (βαθύτερον), one may say about those who came out of the land of Egypt that unexpectedly (παραδόξως) the whole people (λεώς) took up all at once (ἀθρόως), as if God-given (θεοδώρητος), the language called Hebrew; as also one of the prophets among them said: ‘In their coming out of the land of Egypt he heard (ἀκούω) a tongue (γλῶσσα) which he did not know (γινώσκω).’
pass_b_english: It is likewise false that the Hebrews, being Egyptians, had their beginning in a revolt, and false that, in the time of Jesus, others who were Jews revolted against the Jewish commonwealth and followed Jesus. For neither Celsus nor those who think as he does will be able to point to any act of revolt on the part of the Christians.

And yet, if revolt had been the cause of the Christians’ coming together (and they took their beginning from the Jews, who were permitted both to take up arms in defence of their own and to kill their enemies), the lawgiver of the Christians would not have forbidden the killing of a human being altogether, never teaching that any assault by his disciples on another man is just, even if that man is utterly unjust (for he did not think it fitting for his divine legislation to allow the killing of any human being whatever). Nor would Christians, if they had begun from revolt, have accepted laws so exceedingly gentle, under which it was their lot to be slain “like sheep” (Psalm 44:22; Romans 8:36) and never to be able to defend themselves against those who persecuted them.

Moreover, if one examines the matter more deeply, one may say of those who came out of the land of Egypt that the whole people, beyond all expectation, took up all at once the language called Hebrew, as though it were a gift from God. As one of their own prophets said, “When they came out of the land of Egypt, he heard a language he did not know” (Psalm 81:5).

choices.choice: Copy-text: staged source_3.json section 7 (Koetschau 3.7). ‘ὡς πρόβατα’ (being slain ‘like sheep’) echoes LXX Psalm 43:23 (‘we were counted as sheep for slaughter’), which is Psalm 44:22 in English Bibles, as quoted in Romans 8:36; Matthew 10:16 (‘as sheep among wolves’) is a possible secondary echo, not cited inline. The prophet’s words are LXX Psalm 80:6, which is Psalm 81:5 in English Bibles (81:6 in the Hebrew). Origen’s text has the plural ‘αὐτοὺς’ (they came out) but keeps the Psalm’s singular ‘ἔγνω, ἤκουσεν’ (he heard … he did not know); the mixed number is kept (‘he’ = the people, Israel; in the LXX the pronoun refers to Joseph). The lawgiver of the Christians is Christ; his forbidding of all killing is not tied to one verse (compare Matthew 5:21–22, 5:39, 26:52), so it is not cited inline. The Jews’ permission to bear arms and kill enemies reflects the wars of the Law (for example Deuteronomy 20) but is not a verbal allusion; not cited. ‘τὸ κατ᾿ ἀνθρώπου τόλμημα’ rendered ‘any assault … on another man’. ‘μή ποτε δίκαιον εἶναι διδάσκων’ rendered ‘never teaching’. ‘τῇ ἐνθέῳ ἑαυτοῦ νομοθεσίᾳ’ rendered ‘his divine legislation’: the lawgiver is Christ, so ‘inspired’ (which suggests a merely human lawgiver moved by God) is avoided. ‘τὴν ἀρχὴν ἀπὸ Ἰουδαίων εἰληφόσιν’ (dative participle on Χριστιανοῖς) is set in parentheses as a fact stated alongside, not as a cause. ‘τὸ κοινὸν τῶν Ἰουδαίων’ rendered ‘the Jewish commonwealth’, matching 3.5. ‘καίτοι γε’ at the last paragraph introduces a further point and is rendered ‘Moreover’.

‘and they were never able to defend themselves’ made ‘and never to be able to defend themselves’, keeping both infinitives under δι᾿ ὧν … ἐγίνετο
Greek-order clause ‘took up all at once, as though it were a gift from God, the language called Hebrew’ reordered
